item.content:encoded:
This post, while still realted to tech, is not very technical itself. I started this blog with the objetive of writing about subjects I find interesting and practise my writing (and because of that, my texts are LLM free, otherwise it would defeat the purpose right?). I was thinking about extending this to a more general writing. I believe posts will still be related to tech, but, they may be more about things sorounding tech, like this one.

This year, the annual Debian conference was held in my country, presicely in the city of Santa Fe. The first thing that comes to my mind is that it was a really nice that they did not chose City of Buenos Aires for the event. Not because the city is not prepared or is bad in some way, but because almost every tech event is held there. The event was two-week long, I went there for a week and a half.

DebCamp

The DebCamp takes place before the conference week. The objetive is for Debian developers to gather and discuss in person about their Debian-related projects, tasks, etc. This year I started contributing to the Rust team, but unfortunetaly no one from the team was there. Despite of that, it was worth it since I got the chance to meet new people and chat in a quieter environment.

The conference

The conference was full of interesting talks. A typical day started at 10 with multiple talks, a break for lunch at 12, more talks at 14, a coffee break at 16, and then more talks until 18 (with the exception of Wednesday, which was the daytrip day. There were a wide range of topics, and some of the talks were in spanish.

If there was no talk you were interested, you could just go to the hack lab (or go to the silent hack lab if you needed to concentrate). This was really great, since you could mind your own business waiting for the next or check who was near the coffee table (there were a lot of really good coffees from all around the globe) and have a really interesting conversation with somebody.

After 18, people would hang out in the hack lab until around 20 and the go to dinner or the hotel where they were staying.

The social events

There were a few social events organized. I already mentioned the daytrip day, a day off to go and explore the city or some other nice places.

The conference dinner was another official event. We all gathered in a nearby restaurant, pick a table, have some really tasty local food, watch a tango show and dance. On top of all that, the organizers convinced the restaurant manager to migrate his laptop to Debian!

Not all social events were official. For example, some of the local folks prepared a typical argentinian asado for those who did not go to the daytrip tours.

The event I liked the most was the Cheese & Wine party. The premise was that every one (specially the locals) should bring something to eat or drink (not restricted only to wine and cheese, but there was a lot of it anyways) to share. There was A LOT of things from everywhere, not only from Argentina. Beside tasting a lot of rare things from different countries, I got the chance to talk with people from everywhere, so it was a win win situation.

My experience

Developer (or hacker) communities, in my experience, are usually filled with people that are really welcoming and selfless regarding sharing knowledge1. That is something that I’ve always valued.

As in every other place, there were extrovert people and introvert people, but that did not matter much, since everyone was willing talk. Topics varied from deep technical things to common topics like sports, places to visit, etc. Language was not a problem either, people would do a really good effort to communicate effetively (usually in english). In fact, I met someone that speaks 6 (natural) languages, and refused to talk to me in english because he wanted to practise his spanish skills.

If you wanted to talk to someone you had two alternatives, break the ice using the key signing party as an excuse and asking for that person’s signature or use the meet-up board, a physical board where you could put post-it notes to meet with people and discuss specific topics.

My Talk

I had the opportunity to give a talk about Rust (who would have guessed?!). I am starting to get used to talk in front of people, but the jitters just never go away. I had a really good time giving this presentation. You can check it out here (it is in spanish)

Conclusion

If you have the opportunity to assit to an event of this kind do it. Even if you are an introvert like me, it totally worth it. You get to know really interesting people, talk about really interesting topics and try really interesting food from other places.

In the end, even in this strange times we are living with all the AI hype, developer communities are still one of the most welcoming environment for newcommers and a great place to meet people who share similar interets.

  1. Of course there are exceptions, and those exceptions seem to be all gathered in X posting ragebaits (like those who say that AI ‘democratized’ programming when there is a TON of free material to learn about virtually anything related to programming and computer science, but oh surprise, it takes more effort to learn and actually know what you are doing than to write to a chatbox, but that is a discussion for another post). ↩︎
